summary: Describes how to carry iLBC speech inside Real-time Transport Protocol (RTP) packets. It also gives the details for using iLBC with MIME and the Session Description Protocol (SDP). It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3952 explains how to send speech compressed with the iLBC codec over RTP. The compressed data goes into the packet as one or more whole frames with no extra header, and the memo gives the exact layout of a frame so that a receiver can decode it.

questions: how many ilbc frames fit in an rtp packet
what is the ilbc bit rate
how is ilbc carried in rtp
subtitle: How compressed iLBC speech frames are packed into RTP packets, and how two ends agree on the frame size.

tldr.problem: The iLBC codec produces compressed speech frames, but a transport protocol needs to know how to put those frames into packets and how to tell the receiver which frame size is in use.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines an RTP payload format in which the payload is one or more complete iLBC frames with no extra header, and gives the bit layout of a frame, whose bits are ordered in three classes of decreasing sensitivity.
tldr.outcome: It is an Experimental document. It also registers the MIME media type audio/iLBC, defines a file format for stored speech, and fixes how the frame size is negotiated through SDP.

today: RFC 3952 is an Experimental document from December 2004, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the RTP payload format for iLBC speech, registers the audio/iLBC MIME media type, and fixes the file format used to store iLBC speech.

sections.title: Introduction and Background
sections.content:
The memo describes how compressed iLBC speech, as produced by the iLBC codec, may be formatted for use as an RTP payload type. It provides methods to packetize the codec data frames into RTP packets, and the sender may send one or more codec data frames per packet depending on the application scenario, the transport network condition, bandwidth restrictions, delay requirements and packet-loss tolerance.

Global IP Sound developed the iLBC speech compression algorithm for use in IP based communications. The codec enables graceful degradation of speech quality when frames are lost, which happens when IP packets are lost or delayed. The memo says the codec suits real time communications such as telephony and videoconferencing, streaming audio, archival and messaging.

The codec compresses each basic frame of 20 ms or 30 ms of 8000 Hz, 16-bit sampled input speech into output frames with a rate of 400 bits for a 30 ms basic frame and 304 bits for a 20 ms basic frame. It supports two basic frame lengths, 30 ms at 13.33 kbit/s and 20 ms at 15.2 kbit/s, using a block independent linear predictive coding algorithm. When the codec operates at block lengths of 20 ms it produces 304 bits per block, which MUST be packetized in 38 bytes, and for block lengths of 30 ms it produces 400 bits per block, which MUST be packetized in 50 bytes. The memo compares the result to pulse code modulation with packet loss concealment as in ITU-T G.711, which operates at a fixed bit rate of 64 kbit/s, while the codec allows fixed bit rate coding with a quality-versus-bit rate tradeoff close to code-excited linear prediction.
sections.plainLanguage: iLBC compresses speech in short pieces, 20 or 30 milliseconds long, and is built so that a lost piece costs as little quality as possible. The cost is a bit rate of about 13 or 15 kilobits per second instead of the 64 of ordinary telephone audio.

sections.title: The RTP Payload Format
sections.content:
The iLBC codec uses 20 or 30 ms frames and a sampling rate clock of 8 kHz, so the RTP timestamp MUST be in units of 1/8000 of a second. The payload for iLBC has the format shown in the memo's figure: an ordinary RTP header followed by one or more frames of iLBC data. No header specific to this payload format is required.

The RTP header has the expected values described in RFC 3550. The use of the M bit SHOULD follow the applicable RTP profile; RFC 3551, for example, specifies that if the sender does not suppress silence, sending a frame on every frame interval, the M bit will always be zero. When more than one codec data frame is present in a single RTP packet, the timestamp is, as always, the timestamp of the oldest data frame represented in the packet.

The assignment of an RTP payload type is outside the scope of the memo. It is expected that the RTP profile for a particular class of applications will assign a payload type for this encoding, or, if that is not done, that a payload type in the dynamic range shall be chosen by the sender.

More than one iLBC frame may be included in a single RTP packet, but the sender has three restrictions. It SHOULD NOT include more frames in a single packet than will fit in the MTU of the RTP transport protocol. Frames MUST NOT be split between RTP packets. Frames of the different modes, 20 ms and 30 ms, MUST NOT be included within the same packet. The memo says it is RECOMMENDED that the number of frames per packet be consistent with the application: in telephony and other real time applications where delay matters, the delay is lower with fewer frames per packet, while for bandwidth constrained links or delay insensitive streaming, one or more frames per packet would be acceptable.

The number of frames in a packet is not transmitted as part of the payload. The way to determine it is to count the total number of octets in the RTP packet and divide by the number of expected octets per frame.
sections.plainLanguage: The compressed speech goes straight into the packet after the standard RTP header, with nothing added in between. A packet can hold several whole frames, but never half a frame, never frames of two different sizes at once, and never more than the packet size allows.

sections.title: The Bitstream Definition
sections.content:
The total number of bits used to describe one frame of 20 ms speech is 304, which fits in 38 bytes and gives a bit rate of 15.20 kbit/s. For a frame length of 30 ms the total is 400 bits, which fits in 50 bytes and gives a bit rate of 13.33 kbit/s.

In the bitstream definition the bits are distributed into three classes according to their bit error or loss sensitivity. The most sensitive bits, class 1, are placed first in the bitstream for each frame. The less sensitive bits, class 2 follow the class 1 bits, and the least sensitive bits, class 3, are placed at the end of the bitstream for each frame. For the 20 ms and 30 ms frame length cases, the class 1 bits occupy a total of 6 and 8 bytes, which is 48 and 64 bits, the class 2 bits occupy 8 and 12 bytes, which is 64 and 96 bits, and the class 3 bits occupy 24 and 30 bytes, which is 191 and 239 bits. The memo says this distribution of the bits enables the use of uneven level protection. When a quantization index is distributed between more classes, the more significant bits belong to the lowest class.

When packetized into the payload, all the class 1 bits MUST be sorted in order, from top to down, as they were specified in the table, and the same applies to the class 2 and class 3 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Each frame is written out in three blocks. The first block holds the bits that matter most, the last holds the bits that matter least. So if the end of a frame is lost, the part that arrives is still the useful part. The ordering is fixed, so any receiver knows where each block starts.

sections.title: The MIME Type and the Stored File Format
sections.content:
The memo registers one MIME media type, audio/iLBC, with three optional parameters. The maxptime parameter gives the maximum amount of media that can be encapsulated in each packet, expressed in time in milliseconds, calculated as the sum of the time the media in the packet represents, and it should be a multiple of the frame size. The mode parameter gives the iLBC operating frame mode that will be encapsulated in each packet, and its values can be 0, 20 and 30, where 0 is reserved, 20 stands for preferred 20 ms frame size and 30 for preferred 30 ms frame size. The ptime parameter is defined as usual for RTP audio. The memo notes that all of the parameters apply for RTP transfer only.

For stored files the memo defines a storage format. The file begins with a header that includes only a magic number identifying it as an iLBC file, followed by the speech frames in consecutive order. The magic number MUST correspond to the ASCII string #!iLBC30 for the 30 ms frame size mode, or #!iLBC20 for the 20 ms frame size mode. Speech frames lost in transmission MUST be stored as empty frames. The registered file extensions are lbc and LBC, and the intended usage is COMMON, with the expectation that many VoIP applications will use the type.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo also registers the media type for iLBC, with parameters that say the frame size and how much audio a packet may hold, and it defines a plain file format for stored speech. The file starts with a short text marker that says which frame size it uses.

sections.title: Mapping to SDP Parameters
sections.content:
The information in the MIME media type specification maps to fields of the Session Description Protocol. The MIME type goes in the SDP m= line as the media name, the MIME subtype goes in a=rtpmap as the encoding name, the parameters ptime and maxptime go in a=ptime and a=maxptime, and the mode parameter goes in the a=fmtp attribute by copying it directly from the MIME media type string as mode=value. When conveying information by SDP, the encoding name SHALL be iLBC, the same as the MIME subtype.

The memo is explicit that the mode parameter is bi-directional: both sides of a session MUST use the same mode value. The offer contains the preferred mode of the offerer. The answerer may agree by including the same mode in the answer, or may include a different mode. The mode used by both parties SHALL be the lower of the bandwidth modes in the offer and the answer. An offer of mode=20 receiving an answer of mode=30 results in mode=30 being used by both participants, and an offer of mode=30 with an answer of mode=20 also results in mode=30 being used by both. The memo says this matters when one end point uses a bandwidth constrained link, such as a 28.8k modem link or slower, where only the lower frame size will work.

The parameter ptime cannot be used to specify the iLBC operating mode, because for certain values it is impossible to distinguish which mode is about to be used. With ptime=60, for example, it would be impossible to tell whether a packet carries 2 frames of 30 ms or 3 frames of 20 ms. The memo also notes that payload format names are commonly shown in upper case and MIME subtypes in lower case, that both are case-insensitive, and that parameter names are case-insensitive in MIME types and in the default mapping to the SDP a=fmtp attribute.
sections.plainLanguage: The two ends agree on the frame size through the session description. The rule is simple: both sides use the larger frame size, which is the lower bit rate, and that is what lets a slow link still work.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RTP packets using this payload format are subject to the general security considerations of RTP and of any applicable profile. Because the format carries encoded speech, the main security issues are confidentiality and authentication of the speech itself. The payload format has no built-in security mechanisms. Confidentiality of the media streams is achieved by encryption, so external mechanisms such as SRTP MAY be used for that purpose. The data compression used with this payload format is applied end to end, so encryption may be performed after compression with no conflict between the two operations.

The memo also names a potential denial-of-service threat for encodings that have a non-uniform receiver-end computational load, where an attacker injects pathological datagrams that are complex to decode and overload the receiver. It observes that the encodings covered in the document do not exhibit any significant non-uniformity.
sections.plainLanguage: The format itself does nothing to protect the speech. To keep it private, encrypt the RTP stream with something such as SRTP. Compression happens before encryption, so the two do not get in each other's way.

viz.caption: THE THREE CLASSES OF BITS IN AN iLBC FRAME

items.title: Class 1
items.text: The most sensitive bits, placed first: 6 bytes in a 20 ms frame and 8 bytes in a 30 ms frame.

items.title: Class 2
items.text: The middle class, placed after class 1: 8 bytes in a 20 ms frame and 12 bytes in a 30 ms frame.

items.title: Class 3
items.text: The least sensitive bits, placed at the end: 24 bytes in a 20 ms frame and 30 bytes in a 30 ms frame.

items.title: Uneven level protection
items.text: Ordering the bits this way is what lets uneven level protection work.

viz.caption: AN SDP DESCRIPTION OF AN iLBC SESSION IN 20 MS MODE

data.title: Session description
data.code:
m=audio 49120 RTP/AVP 97
a=rtpmap:97 iLBC/8000
a=fmtp:97 mode=20
